title: The baseline that tied us
subtitle: Retiring a flattering benchmark, building the strongest retriever I could, and publishing the result that hurt

stats.label: points of recall the first headline claimed, struck before publication
held-out queries, frozen before any model result was reported
embedding models in the bake-off for the baseline

lede: My tool-discovery model had a headline: a large lead in recall over classical retrieval. The results were about to be written up and every incentive pointed at believing the number. I struck it. The comparison was against a weak baseline, and a weak baseline makes any model look good. I replaced it with the strongest classical retriever I could assemble. That retriever tied the model at the cutoffs that matter and beat it on long, buried requests. The tie is the number I publish. The first comparison for the capabilities model was against an external small tool-calling model whose results carried no information: anything would have won.
quote: A result I would not accept from someone else is a result I cannot publish.
evidence: ML evaluation methodology: a 469-query held-out set frozen before any model result was reported, plus fifteen long, buried requests.
Benchmark integrity: a 17-point recall headline struck before publication because its baseline had ranked two thousand entries against the model's forty-two.
Hybrid retrieval baselines: a dense-plus-BM25 fusion retriever with every weight and cutoff chosen by sweep, which tied the model and beat it on buried requests.
Embedding model selection: a bake-off of 5 embedding models that replaced an incumbent chosen by habit.
Known-answer controls in experiment harnesses: a control that failed once stopped the whole matrix until a numerical precision setting was pinned and every ranker re-run.
author: Corey James
